background.definition: Hypertensive emergencies are defined as severe elevations of blood pressure (BP) over 180/120 mm Hg complicated by impending or progressive target organ damage.Hypertensive emergencies include hypertensive channelopathy, intracerebral hemorrhage, acute myocardial infarction or unstable angina pectoris, acute left ventricular failure with pulmonary edema, dissecting aortic aneurysm (thoracic or abdominal) and eclampsia. Hypertensive urgencies are severe elevations of BP without progressive target organ dysfunction.

list.listitem: About 1 to 3 patients per 100,000 persons per year develop hypertensive crises.
The annual incidence is about 1.7 (±0.7) per 100,000 for white patients compared with 7.3 (±4.6) per 100,000 for black patients.
Hypertensive urgencies and emergencies account for as many as 25% of all medical urgencies and emergencies at an emergency department in Italy.
Uncontrolled essential hypertension or secondary hypertension is the main cause of hypertensive crisis.
Since access to care is a critical aspect of treatment, disadvantaged patients are at the greatest risk.
During a hypertensive emergency, the rapid elevation of BP is due to failure of normal autoregulation and sudden increases in systemic vascular resistance.

At the same time, there is endovascular injury with fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles, leading to a cycle of ischemia, platelet deposition and further failure of autoregulation as vasoactive substances are released.

In a hypertensive emergency, autoregulation is altered, lowering the threshold for hypoperfusion of brain and other vital organs if the BP is abruptly lowered. Thus, rapid BP lowering in an emergency is dangerous.
Markers of coagulation, fibrinolysis, platelet- and endothelial activation, as well as inflammation are increased in hypertensive crisis.
Proper control of underlying hypertension is the key to preventing hypertensive crises. C

Base the testing on the patient’s presenting circumstances. At a minimum, perform the following tests: electrolytes, renal function tests, UA, and ECG. C

Hypertensive emergencies are severe elevations in BP (>180/120) with evidence of impending or progressive target organ damage, while hypertensive urgencies are severe elevations in BP without progressive target organ dysfunction.

About 75% of patients with hypertensive emergencies present with either headache or vision changes, and about 40% present with GI complaints, mostly nausea and vomiting. In addition, these patients may present with with chest pain (27%), dyspnea (22%), and neurologic deficit (21%).
Patients with hypertensive emergency may have signs and symptoms of cerebral infarction (24%), acute pulmonary edema (23%), encephalopathy (16%), and cerebral hemorrhage (4.5%).
Patients with hypertensive urgencies, on the other hand, present slightly differently. Many are asymptomatic, although they may also have headache (22%), epistaxis (17%), and faintness (10%).

Patients with hypertensive emergencies require rapid assessment and stabilization. Testing should be based on the patient’s presenting circumstances. At a minimum, perform the following tests: electrolytes, renal function tests, UA, and ECG.
Order a CXR for patients complaining of dyspnea or chest pain as well as a work-up for pulmonary edema, dissecting aortic aneurysm, and acute coronary syndromes.
Order CT of the brain in patients with headache, altered mental status, or other neurologic symptoms.
Order imaging for dissecting abdominal aortic aneurysm in patients with abdominal pain.
Patients often present with chest pain, dyspnea, neurologic signs, and headache.
At a minimum, order electrolytes, renal function tests, UA, and ECG.
Hypertensive emergencies are medical emergencies and require rapid evaluation and immediate BP reduction ().

Patients with acute ischemic stroke do not benefit from immediate hypertensive treatment. B
If tolerated, lower the systolic BP to less than 100 mm Hg in patients with aortic dissection. C
Treat patients who have hypertensive urgencies with oral short-acting agents (ie, captopril, labetalol, clonidine) and observe for several hours. Clinical trial data are lacking. C
Treat patients who have hypertensive emergencies with parenteral medications.

Treat patients who have hypertensive urgencies with oral short-acting agents (ie, captopril, labetalol, clonidine) and observe for several hours.
Because it can cause excessive drops in BP precipitating renal, cerebral, or coronary ischemia, Do not use short-acting nifedipine in the initial management of hypertensive crises.
A Cochrane review identified 15 RCTs with 869 patients of 7 drug classes. Clinical outcomes were not well reported and there is no evidence to support one drug class over another.
Since hypertensive urgencies are usually due to lack of adherence to medication, it is important to explore the barriers to treatment.
Admit patients with hypertensive emergencies to the ICU for continuous monitoring and IV therapy.

Patients who have no signs of end-organ damage and an established primary care physician may be discharged from the emergency department with rapid follow-up to recheck and modify the antihypertensive treatment.
Patients presenting with hypertensive urgency do not necessarily benefit from hospialization.
No studies have been able to identify the optimal rate of BP lowering in hypertensive emergencies or urgencies.
The initial goal is to reduce mean arterial BP by 25% within minutes to 1 hour.
If the patient is stable, then lower the BP to 160/100-110 within the next 2 to 6 hours.
If the initial management is well tolerated, reduction to normal levels can be achieved over the next 24 to 48 hours.
Patients with acute ischemic stroke do not benefit from immediate hypertensive treatment.
In patients with aortic dissection, lower the systolic BP to under 100 mm Hg if tolerated.

In hypertensive urgencies, there is no evidence that failure to lower BP aggressively in the emergency department results in increased short-term risk to the patient. C
The prognosis in hypertensive urgency is good, with only 1 CV event per 1000 patients in the week following presentation.
The 4-year survival of hypertensive emergencies is about 90%.
Prompt management of hypertensive emergencies is key to limiting morbidity and mortality associated with target organ damage.
CAUTION: excessive falls in BP can lead to renal, cerebral, or coronary ischemia.
The 4-year survival of hypertensive emergencies is about 90%.

About 20% of patients will wind up on dialysis within 4 years after hypertensive emergencies. The two strongest predictors of renal failure are the baseline creatinine and the presence of secondary hypertension.

In hypertensive urgencies, there is no evidence that failure to lower BP aggressively in the emergency department results in increased short-term risk to the patient. The prognosis is good, with only 1 CV event per 1000 patients in the week following presentation.
Elevated troponin levels suggests a greater long-term risk of cardiovascular complications in subjects with hypertensive crisis.
Communication among the emergency department physicians, hospital attending physicians, and the patient’s primary care physician are important in establishing appropriate follow-up.
Patients with hypertensive urgencies should be followed up by their primary care provider in 1 to 2 days to address long-term management.
Educate patients about target organ damage and the importance of treating and monitoring their hypertension.
Preeclampsia and eclampsia are covered in another chapter.

feature.caption: Parenteral Drugs for Managing Hypertensive Emergencies (All Regimens May Cause Hypotension; Use with Care).
feature.feature_body:
Parenteral Drugs for Hypertensive Emergency Treatment
Dose Onset of Action Duration of Action Adverse Effects Special Indications
Vasodilators
Sodium nitroprusside 0.25-10 μg/kg/min IV infusion Immediate 1-2 min Nausea, vomiting, muscle twitching, sweating, thiocyanate, and cyanide intoxication Most hypertensive emergencies; caution with high intracranial pressure or azotemia
Nicardipine hydrochloride 5-15 mg/h IV 5-10 min 15-30 min, may exceed 4 h Tachycardia, headache, flushing, local phlebitis Most hypertensive emergencies except acute heart failure; caution with coronary ischemia
Fenoldopam mesylate 0.1-0.3 μg/kg/min IV infusion <5 min 30 min Tachycardia, headache, nausea, flushing Most hypertensive emergencies; caution with glaucoma
Nitroglycerin medication 5-100 μg/min IV infusion 2-5 min 5-10 min Headache, vomiting, methemoglobinemia, tolerance with prolonged use Coronary ischemia
Enalaprilat 1.25-5 mg IV every 6 h 15-30 min 6-12 h Precipitous fall in pressure in high-renin states; variable response Acute left ventricular failure; avoid in acute myocardial infarction
Hydralazine hydrochloride 10-20 mg IV 10-20 min IV 1-4 h IV Tachycardia, flushing, headache, vomiting, aggravation of angina Eclampsia
10-40 mg IM 20-30 min IM 4-6 h IM
Adrenergic Inhibitors
Labetalol hydrochloride 20-80 mg IV bolus every 10 min, 0.5-2.0 mg/min IV infusion 5-10 min 3-6 h Nausea and vomiting, scalp tingling, bronchoconstriction, dizziness, heart block, orthostatic hypotension Most hypertensive emergencies, except acute heart failure
Esmolol hydrochloride 250-500 μg/kg/min IV bolus, then 50-100 μg/kg/min by infusion; may repeat bolus after 5 min or may increase infusion to 300 μg/min 1-2 min 10-30 min Hypotension, nausea, asthma, first-degree heart block, heart failure Aortic dissection, perioperative
Phentolamine 5-15 mg IV bolus 1-2 min 10-30 min Tachycardia, flushing, headache Catecholamine excess
